item.title: BrainPro: Process-conditioned Pretraining with Topographic Retrieval for Large EEG Models
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Yi Ding, Muyun Jiang, Weibang Jiang, Shuailei Zhang, Xinliang Zhou, Chenyu Liu, Shanglin Li, Yong Li, Cuntai Guan
arXiv:2509.22050v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: EEG foundation models are pretrained on heterogeneous corpora, but two challenges remain underexplored: (1) experimental protocols provide mental-process cues that are rarely used in masked pretraining, and (2) electrode montages vary across datasets, making spatial representations montage-dependent. Existing methods typically learn a single general-purpose representation and model spatial structure implicitly, limiting their ability to exploit process-related information under montage heterogeneity. We introduce BrainPro, a process-conditioned self-supervised pretraining framework that couples topographic retrieval with shared and process-associated representation learning. BrainPro maps dataset-specific montages to a universal channel-region template and retrieves channel- and region-level spatial filters to form a topographically aligned spatial basis. Over this basis, BrainPro learns a shared encoder for general EEG structure and additional affective, motor-related, and auxiliary residual branches for process-associated variation. Protocol-derived mental-process cues condition branch activation and region-weighted masked reconstruction, incorporating topographic spatial priors and process information. Across nine public BCI benchmarks, BrainPro achieves strong performance among evaluated baselines. Ablations, channel-drop analysis, encoder-configuration studies, and spatial-filter visualizations suggest that topographic retrieval and process-conditioned representation learning jointly improve EEG decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/yi-ding-cs/BrainPro.

item.title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Jiahao Huang, Jun Wang
arXiv:2611.26590v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.

item.title: Before the Choice: An Evidential Framework for Studying Prospective Representations in Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Sion Israel Sion
arXiv:2611.25170v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An observable decision reveals the selected action but does not determine which alternatives were internally represented. Drawing on prospection research and hippocampal forward-sweep observations, we develop Before the Choice, an evidence-oriented framework distinguishing future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. Code and protocol records: https://github.com/besionisrael/before-choice

item.title: When spike sorting matters: single-neuron identity in the quantification of neural circuits
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Suarez-Barrera, D., Encinas-Rodriguez, N., Diaz, H., Zainos, A., Bayones, L., Rossi-Pool, R.
Multiunit threshold crossings support high-performance brain-computer interfaces and preserve the low-dimensional trajectories that summarize population dynamics, raising the question of when spike sorting is still necessary. Using previously published recordings from four rhesus monkeys, we analyzed areas 3b and 1 of primary somatosensory cortex and ventral premotor cortex during a bimodal detection task, and ventral premotor cortex during an interval comparison task. From the same spikes, we built three representations: putative single units obtained with nonlinear sorting (UMAP and HDBSCAN), intermingled units obtained with linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit activity. Nonlinear sorting resolved up to three times more units than multiunit activity. In area 1, mixing discarded the periodicity information carried by phase-locked neurons, lengthened intrinsic timescales by about 40%, increased trial-to-trial variability, and raised neurometric detection thresholds by 33%. In premotor cortex, mixing reduced the task-related information recovered from the population and hid significant dimensions of its dynamics. After geometric alignment, the overall shape of population trajectories was nearly identical across representations, but distances between population states were distorted, and the approximately linear representation of interval duration saturated for longer intervals. Multiunit activity is therefore sufficient for analyses that rely on the dominant, shared structure of population activity, such as decoding, whereas analyses of single-neuron coding, variability, timescales, dimensionality, and parametric representations often require spike sorting.

item.title: Implicit Neural Representations of Individual Behavior
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Andrew Kang, Priya Narasimhan
arXiv:2606.12200v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study policy representation learning from unlabeled multi-policy behavioral data. Each episode is generated by a fixed policy, but policy labels are unavailable. This setting appears in robotics play, demonstrations, games, racing, and other datasets where heterogeneous behaviors are mixed without annotations. We introduce Behavioral INR, a self-supervised generative model that adapts implicit neural representations (INRs) from vision to behavior. Instead of mapping coordinates to RGB values, Behavioral INR represents a policy as a state-action function mapping states to subsequent actions. An episode-level latent modulates this function through FiLM layers, yielding a generative prior over policies and allowing policy identity to be inferred without supervision. Because INRs treat each datapoint as samples from an underlying function, the same model naturally accommodates variable episode lengths and different sampling granularities, as in vision INRs with different image resolutions. We also define policy-level out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts along state-distribution and action-distribution axes, which arise when policies overlap in states or actions but are not captured by standard behavioral OOD settings based only on new agents or environments. We evaluate on synthetic Gaussian random field data, MuJoCo demonstrations with controlled OOD splits, and real-world chess, Formula 1 racing, robotics, and Seek-Avoid datasets. Behavioral INR most consistently improves policy identifiability in the hardest continuous state-action settings, especially when longer episodes, more policies, and OOD splits reduce the usefulness of marginal shortcuts; amortized history encoders remain competitive when policy identity can be recovered from symbolic repetition or low-dimensional action statistics.

item.title: Trial history and model-derived reward prediction errors in mousevisual decisions
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Mirabedini, A., JanatAbadi, R., Khanteymoori, A.
A reward prediction error (RPE) estimated from an animal's behavior can predict its next choice. Part of this predictive value may come from information about earlier trials that a choice model could also use directly. We asked whether a model-derived RPE improves choice prediction beyond the observable history of stimuli, choices, and rewards. We analyzed 275,292 trials from 107 mice performing the International Brain Laboratory visual decision task and evaluated the main choice models on sessions that were not used for fitting. Recent choices strongly improved prediction. An RPE based on a stimulus-dependent reward expectation added a small gain beyond the preceding choice and reward, and this gain fell to near zero once the model included the preceding stimulus. When the model also summarized choices and rewards over several earlier trials, an RPE trace with the same retention parameter as the history traces did not reliably improve prediction. In simulated agents with known decision rules, a simplified version of this comparison detected an RPE-based learning rule in which choices depended on accumulated prediction errors, and did not improve prediction for an agent that used trial history directly. In mice, the state-dependent RPE and its trace added little predictive information beyond observable trial history, which limits what choice prediction alone can reveal about prediction-error learning.

item.title: Hierarchical Latent Structure Learning through Online Inference
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Ines Aitsahalia, Kiyohito Iigaya
arXiv:2603.19139v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning systems must balance generalization across experiences with discrimination of task-relevant details. Effective learning therefore requires representations that support both. Online latent-cause models support incremental inference but assume flat partitions, whereas hierarchical Bayesian models capture multilevel structure but typically require offline inference. We introduce the \textbf{Hierarchical Online Learning of Multiscale Experience Structure (HOLMES) model}, a computational framework for hierarchical latent structure learning through online inference. HOLMES combines a variation on the nested Chinese Restaurant Process prior with sequential Monte Carlo inference to perform tractable trial-by-trial inference over hierarchical latent representations without explicit supervision over the latent structure. In simulations, HOLMES matched the predictive performance of flat models while learning more compact representations that supported one-shot backward transfer to higher-level latent categories. In a forward transfer task, HOLMES additionally achieved above-chance outcome prediction for stimuli with never-before-seen feature combinations, by exploiting abstract shape-level representations learned across diverse training instances. These results provide a tractable computational framework for discovering hierarchical structure in sequential data.

item.title: Overexpression of α synuclein in Midbrain Dopamine Neurons Drives Learning Deficits in Mice
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Coutant, B., Zhuang, X., Seiler, J., Nadel, J., Romo, K., Fu, Y., Edwards, R. L., Halliday, G., Lerner, T., Nelson, A. B.
Parkinson disease (PD) is diagnosed based on core motor features. However, changes in cognitive function are often already present. Cognitive symptoms include changes in executive function, including organization, planning, multi-tasking, and flexible decision-making. These early cognitive deficits have been difficult to model and remain understudied. Here, we investigated whether AAV-based overexpression of wild-type human alpha-synuclein (syn) in midbrain dopaminergic neurons can produce deficits in learning and behavioral flexibility. We found that syn mice develop progressive impairment in basic action-outcome learning. In addition, we found that syn mice show impairments in behavioral flexibility during probabilistic reversal learning. Together, these findings demonstrate that syn overexpression in midbrain dopaminergic neurons is sufficient to drive cognitive decline. Our early-stage PD model offers a temporal window to dissect cellular and circuits mechanisms underlying non-motor manifestations of PD.

item.title: Neural mechanisms of lightness constancy
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Didehvar, F., Vanstiphout, R., Cavanagh, P., Franken, T. P.
Object-specific variables are entangled in sensory input. For example, lightness, whether a surface is white or black, not only depends on the surface reflectance but also on the incident illumination. The brain must thus perform inference to achieve a reliable percept of lightness irrespective of illumination (lightness constancy). Whether this results from simple luminance contrast operations early in the visual system or computations at higher levels remains unresolved. We find that neural lightness signals only appear in the extragranular layers of cortical Area V4, and dominate for shadow regions, as opposed to the comparison of local and surrounding luminance (simultaneous contrast). This suggests that lightness is computed downstream from simultaneous contrast, ruling out simple low-level mechanisms, and instead supporting mid-level anchoring theory.

item.title: Motor learning engages intrinsic plasticity in the human cortex
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Clennell, B., Luo, B., Lam, K. T., Hu, Y., Peterchev, A. V., Hannah, R.
Learning is commonly explained by changes in synaptic strength. In animals, however, learning also engages intrinsic plasticity -- changes in how readily neurons convert synaptic input into firing. Its contribution to human learning has been unclear, because conventional non-invasive measures of cortical excitability primarily reflect synaptic strength. Here we used controllable-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, before and after motor training. Training produced signatures of increased intrinsic excitability, selectively in the cortical representation of the trained muscle, but not an untrained muscle. Individuals showing larger intrinsic excitability changes learned faster, independently of changes in motor-evoked potential amplitude, an index of synaptic excitability that increased following training but did not predict learning rate. An axon model reproduced the measured changes through small shifts in membrane excitability. These findings provide evidence that intrinsic plasticity is expressed in the intact human brain, and that it represents a behaviourally relevant component of learning-related cortical adaptation.

item.title: Beyond the court: Sport-specific differences in visuomotor brain networks in female volleyball athletes
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: SocArXiv
Lena Schatz et al.
Physical activity is increasingly associated not only with physiological adaptations but also with cognitive effects. Complex, interactive sports such as soccer and volleyball place high demands on visual perception, spatial orientation, and rapid decision-making. Athletes in these disciplines outperform non-athletes in visuospatial attention and executive control, yet it remains unclear whether sport-specific cognitive demands are reflected in the structural connectivity of visual and visuomotor white matter pathways. It is also unknown whether sports with similarly high visuomotor demands show comparable patterns that jointly distinguish them from non-athletic controls. This study uses diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to examine structural differences in visual and visuomotor fiber tracts between female volleyball players, female soccer players, and a non-athletic control group. The focus is on cortical tracts as well as tracts in the pons and cerebellum, particularly corticopontocerebellar connections, which are thought to play a central role in the fine-tuning of complex movements. We expect both athlete groups to show altered diffusion parameters in visually and fine-motor relevant tracts compared to controls, with no meaningful differences between the two athlete groups. The study has a prospective cross-sectional design with group comparisons and no intervention. A new sample of 35 semi-professional female volleyball players (aged 18–35) will be recruited and measured at a single time point, including T1-weighted structural MRI, a diffusion-weighted sequence (DTI), a resting-state scan, and questionnaires (General Depression Scale [ADS], Perceived Stress Scale [PSS], and demographic, health- and exercise-related data). Data from female soccer players and non-athletic controls come from previously conducted studies. In the long term, the findings may advance our understanding of the neurobiological basis of sport-specific cognitive-motor expertise and inform future research on training, talent development, and cognitive-motor rehabilitation.

item.title: Does transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation increase perceived direct retrieval of autobiographical memory? A sham-controlled within-subject crossover study
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: SocArXiv
Noboru Matsumoto
This study tests whether transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) makes autobiographical memory retrieval feel more direct, sudden, and effortless than sham stimulation, using a within-subject comparison. Whether a memory is judged to have been retrieved directly or generatively depends not only on retrieval latency and cue concreteness but also on subjective feelings (Uzer et al., 2012). Matsumoto et al. (2022) showed that individuals with higher interoceptive sensibility report more direct retrieval, and that this association is mediated by bodily and emotional reactions during retrieval. This finding fits a predictive-processing account in which a large interoceptive prediction error at retrieval makes a memory feel as though it came to mind suddenly and directly. However, the evidence so far is correlational. In an 8-week mindfulness intervention designed to train interoception (Matsumoto et al., 2026), direct retrieval judgments unexpectedly decreased and retrieval effort increased. Inter-beat intervals (IBIs) immediately before the memory response were shorter on trials judged as direct retrieval, but this physiological response did not change with the intervention. The present study therefore uses taVNS, which modulates afferent visceral pathways through the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, to test experimentally whether manipulating the interoceptive system changes subjective judgments of retrieval mode. On a single day, participants receive both taVNS and sham stimulation (order counterbalanced) and complete an Autobiographical Memory Test (AMT) with 10 positive and 10 negative cue words under each condition. The primary outcomes are direct retrieval judgments, retrieval suddenness, and retrieval effort. The secondary outcomes are retrieval latency and memory specificity. Phenomenological characteristics of the memories and IBIs immediately before the memory response are examined as exploratory outcomes.

item.title: Measuring Temporal Self-Reference: registered first-pass test of the predicted five-metric signatures on public EEG data
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: SocArXiv
klaus syha
Summary (paste into the OSF "Summary" / "Description" field): Registered test of the predictions of "Measuring Temporal Self-Reference: Quantitative Predictions for Disorders of Thinking" (K. Syha, March 2026, corrected version). Five EEG metrics in nats (temporal mutual information TMI(tau), recurrence density rho, decay half-life tau_1/2, effective dimensionality d_eff, SNR_TMI) are computed with frozen, calibrated code on three public datasets: RepOD schizophrenia (14 patients, 14 controls), IEEE DataPort ADHD (61 children with ADHD, 60 controls), OpenNeuro ds004504 (36 AD, 23 FTD, 29 controls). For schizophrenia, ADHD and AD the observed five-metric signature (z-scored against the dataset's controls) is tested against the predicted signature of the paper's Table 1, coded as numbers: (a) match (cosine above a 10,000-permutation null), (b) specificity (closer to its own signature than to any other), (c) the defining metric in the predicted direction (one-sided Mann-Whitney, p < 0.05), (d) for AD, d_eff correlated with MMSE. A signature counts as confirmed if (a), (b) and (c) hold. Secondary: the same with TMI in excess of spectrum-matched surrogates (spectral confound), DET, participation ratio, FTD (exploratory). None of the metrics has been computed on any of these datasets, and the datasets have not been downloaded for this analysis. The attached PDF gives the full registration; the attached JSON the SHA-256 hashes of the frozen code (MIT licence). Foreknowledge field: Data exist (public datasets), but no part of them has been analysed with these metrics, and they have not been downloaded for this analysis at the time of registration. Other measures have been published on these datasets by others. item.title: Assessing the criterion validity of attentional control measures
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: SocArXiv
Julia M. Haaf et al.
The current preregistration is an extension of an existing preregistration. In the existing one, the study information is described (see https://osf.io/duqyk/overview). Here, the project is extended using additional statistical analyses. The current preregistration therefore mainly describes these additional analyses. Previous research has highlighted two challenges when measuring attentional control: 1. the difficulty of isolating attentional control from measurement error, and 2. the neglect of individual differences in the speed-accuracy trade-off (see Rey-Mermet et al., 2026 for an overview). The goal of the additional analyses is to overcome these challenges. To this end, we propose two additional modeling approaches: A Bayesian hierarchical linear model and a Bayesian hierarchical diffusion model. Their main advantage is that measurement error is optimally taken into account. Furthermore, the second model has the advantage of taking the speed-accuracy trade-off into account.
